# Scenario analyses and budget impact -- ciNPWT after instrumented posterior lumbar fusion

> **VERIFIED RESULTS -- Phase A2 full-text verification completed 2026-08-17: 46 of 48 parameters were closed out against the 14 source full texts and 43 carry a table/page locator; 2 remain unresolvable assumptions (the ciNPWT institutional net acquisition price and the superficial tunnel length). SSI/ciNPWT risk-threshold Markov CUA; US commercial payer; 2025 USD; monthly cycles; 24-cycle base horizon; 3%/yr discounting; WTP $100000/QALY.**

*Generated by `run_scenarios.py` from the read-only engine (`inputs.py` / `model.py`); no parameter value is owned by this script. Model-based result; not a substitute for clinical evidence.*

Every scenario is run at all three reported risk strata -- low **p = 2.0%** (Freire-Archer [17]), intermediate **p = 6.6%** (Edmiston [12]), high **p = 11.4%** (Mueller [6]) -- except where the scenario is itself a risk statement (decolonization), where the stratum value is treated as the *pre*-decolonization risk and the model is run at the residual. Increments are **`B_cinpwt` minus `A_standard`**; INMB is at **$100,000/QALY** unless stated.

## Decision stability -- the question that matters

Point estimates move in every scenario; what decides practice is whether the **sign of INMB** changes. In the base case ciNPWT is *dominant* (cheaper and better) at all three strata, so a sign flip means INMB turns **negative** -- ciNPWT stops being worth using at that risk level.

**7 scenario x stratum cells flip the sign of INMB**, spread over 5 scenarios:

| Scenario | Stratum | p | INMB @ $100k | Base-case INMB | Dominance |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `effect_superficial_only` | low | 2.00% | **-$209** | $155 | ciNPWT more costly & more effective |
| `effect_superficial_only` | intermediate | 6.60% | **-$115** | $1,086 | ciNPWT more costly & more effective |
| `effect_superficial_only` | high | 11.40% | **-$18** | $2,057 | ciNPWT more costly & more effective |
| `medicare_6mo_horizon` | low | 2.00% | **-$49** | $155 | ciNPWT more costly & more effective |
| `rr_attenuated` | low | 2.00% | **-$94** | $155 | ciNPWT more costly & more effective |
| `horizon_90d` | low | 2.00% | **-$17** | $155 | ciNPWT more costly & more effective |
| `decol_residual_attenuated` | low | 1.60% | **-$126** | $155 | ciNPWT more costly & more effective |

Read by stratum: **low** 5 flip(s); **intermediate** 1 flip(s); **high** 1 flip(s). The pattern is the substantive finding -- the decision is fragile only where the baseline risk is low, because the whole value of ciNPWT is the SSI cost it averts, and at low risk there is little to avert against a device toll that is charged to every patient.

### A weaker decision change: cost-effective but no longer cost-saving

In the base case ciNPWT is **dominant** -- it costs less *and* gains QALYs -- at every stratum, so no budget-holder has to weigh a price against a QALY at all. A scenario can take that away without turning INMB negative: ciNPWT then remains cost-**effective** at $100,000/QALY while ceasing to be cost-**saving**. That is a materially different conversation with a payer and is reported separately from the sign flips above (`cost_saving` column in `scenarios_results.csv`).

| Scenario | Stratum | Inc. cost | ICER | INMB @ $100k | Status |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `deep_frac_030` | low | **+$25** | $74,823/QALY | $8 | ciNPWT more costly & more effective |

The attribution-adjusted row is the one to note: at low risk, halving the SSI-attributable cost is enough to make ciNPWT a net *purchase* rather than a net *saving*, even though it still buys QALYs at well under $100,000 each.

## Horizons -- which SSI cost tranches are charged

SSI cost enters as **three marginal Edmiston tranches** charged at the cycle of onset and at onset **+6** and **+12** cycles. Onset is confined to the first 90 days, so entrants occupy `SUP_0`/`DEEP_0` at cycles 1-3 and the three tranches land at cycles **1-3**, **7-9** and **13-15**. A toll falling beyond the horizon is not charged. This is by design (BUILD-CONTRACT section 6.2), not truncation error:

| Horizon | Cycles | Tranche 1 (1-3) | Tranche 2 (7-9) | Tranche 3 (13-15) | Cost per SSI charged (2025 USD) |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---:|
| 90 d | 3 | **charged** | not charged | not charged | $28,534 |
| 6 mo | 6 | **charged** | not charged | not charged | $28,534 |
| 1 y | 12 | **charged** | **charged** | not charged | $35,876 |
| 2 y (base case) | 24 | **charged** | **charged** | **charged** | $44,784 |
| 5 y | 60 | **charged** | **charged** | **charged** | $44,784 |

**The 1-year row is the trap.** Tranche 2 lands at cycles 7-9, comfortably *inside* a 12-cycle horizon, and **is** charged; only tranche 3 is not. Dropping it would silently remove $15,109 (deep) / $6,137 (superficial) in 2019 USD from every 1-year row and would look like a plausible horizon effect rather than a bug. The selection here is driven off `model.tranches_charged()` / `model.ssi_cost_per_case(horizon_cycles=)`, which raises on a horizon that clips a tranche, rather than a hand-written filter.

### The 5-year row is identical to the 2-year row, and that is correct

In the base case the 5-year result reproduces the 2-year result **exactly** (measured max deviation: incremental cost 0.00e+00, incremental QALY 1.11e-15, INMB 1.11e-10 -- asserted in `run_scenarios.py`, not merely observed). Four structural facts force it:

1. the SSI hazard is **zero after 90 days**, so no new event can occur after cycle 3;
2. all three cost tranches are charged by **cycle 15**;
3. both tunnels drain into `RECOV` by cycle 16, so no utility decrement survives past cycle 16; and
4. from there both arms hold **identical alive mass in states of identical utility** (`RECOV` = `WELL` in the base case), because mortality does not depend on state.

So the 5-year row is **not** a redundant copy-paste, and it is **not** evidence that the horizon is irrelevant. It is evidence that under full recovery the model has nothing left to say after two years. The 5-year horizon becomes informative **only** through the residual-decrement scenario, where `RECOV` utility differs from `WELL` and the two arms therefore diverge for every remaining cycle:

| Stratum | 2 y, full recovery | 5 y, full recovery | 2 y, residual 0.02 | 5 y, residual 0.02 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| low | $155 | $155 | $204 | **$325** |
| intermediate | $1,086 | $1,086 | $1,247 | **$1,649** |
| high | $2,057 | $2,057 | $2,335 | **$3,030** |

The first two columns are equal by construction; the last two are not. That contrast **is** the horizon result and is the only honest way to report a 5-year row in this model.

## Medicare perspective -- the required footnote

Weighted 24-month incremental cost per SSI: **$44,784** commercial vs **$35,004** Medicare (2025 USD, deep fraction 0.745).

**A2 RETIRED THIS FOOTNOTE (2026-08-17).** Until the full-text verification gate this section stated that Edmiston reports the Medicare *superficial* payment at 6 months only, and that the 12- and 24-month Medicare superficial tranches were `derived_assumption` extrapolations transferring the commercial growth ratio onto the reported 6-month value. **All three Medicare superficial payments are reported** -- $11,044, $17,967 and $24,096 -- in Edmiston's Abstract, Results, Table 3 and Discussion. The correct marginal tranches are $6,923 and $6,129, each roughly twice the extrapolated values this build used ($3,259 and $3,124). The extrapolation also failed in principle: Medicare payments grow FASTER than commercial between 6 and 12 months (1.627 vs 1.295), so a transferred commercial ratio understates them.

**Every dollar in the Medicare row is now a reported Edmiston value**, and the four-tranche identity closes exactly: 11,044 + 6,923 + 6,129 = 24,096. Superficial SSI contributes 10.1% of the weighted Medicare 24-month cost per SSI at a superficial fraction of 0.255. No tranche in this row is extrapolated, so no extrapolation footnote is required anywhere the row appears.

`medicare_6mo_horizon` (6 cycles) is retained, but its rationale has changed: it was the clean fallback that avoided the extrapolated tranches, and since there are no extrapolated tranches it is now simply a horizon sensitivity. At 6 cycles only tranche 1 (cycles 1-3) is charged and no tranche is clipped, so read it as a floor rather than a like-for-like substitute:

| Stratum | Medicare 2 y | Medicare 6 mo | Commercial 2 y (base case) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| low | $79 | -$49 | $155 |
| intermediate | $837 | $413 | $1,086 |
| high | $1,627 | $894 | $2,057 |

## Decolonization -- the secondary analysis, in one line

Universal *S. aureus* decolonization is background in **both** arms (SHEA/IDSA essential practice for implant procedures), so both its cost (~$60) and its effect **cancel exactly** from every base-case increment. It survives only as a secondary analysis, and the plan specifies exactly one transparent line for it:

```
residual-risk multiplier = (1 - f_SA) + f_SA x OR_decol
                        = (1 - 0.46) + 0.46 x 0.56
                        = 0.54 + 0.2576
                        = 0.7976
```

using an *S. aureus* fraction of spine-SSI organisms of **46%** (Freire-Archer 2023 [17]) and the spine-specific combined CHG + mupirocin odds ratio **0.56** (Joshi 2026 [2]). Only the *S. aureus* share of the SSI pool is assumed to respond; the remaining 54% is left untouched, which is why the multiplier is 0.798 and not 0.56.

**How far does decolonization shift patients below the ciNPWT threshold?** The ciNPWT break-even risk is a threshold on the risk the patient actually carries *into* the ciNPWT decision -- i.e. on the **residual** risk. Decolonization multiplies that residual by 0.798, so expressed on the **pre-decolonization** risk scale the same break-even sits at `p* / 0.798`:

| Threshold, base-case reporting settings | Residual-risk scale | Pre-decolonization risk scale |
|---|---:|---:|
| ciNPWT break-even `p*` (2 y, 3%/yr, WTP $100,000) | **1.235%** | **1.549%** |
| with attenuated effect RR = 0.85 | 3.211% | 4.026% |

So decolonization moves the required baseline risk **up by a factor 1.2538 (+25.4%)**: patients whose pre-decolonization 90-day risk lies between **1.235%** and **1.549%** cleared the ciNPWT threshold before decolonization and fall below it afterwards. That band is narrow in absolute terms because the threshold itself is low -- the honest reading is that decolonization removes only a thin sliver of patients from ciNPWT eligibility, not that it displaces ciNPWT.

| Stratum | Pre-decolonization p | Residual p (x 0.798) | INMB at pre-decol p | INMB at residual p | INMB at residual p, RR 0.85 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| low | 2.00% | 1.60% | $155 | $73 | -$126 |
| intermediate | 6.60% | 5.26% | $1,086 | $815 | $160 |
| high | 11.40% | 9.09% | $2,057 | $1,590 | $458 |

**Limitation, stated rather than buried.** The residual SSI pool after decolonization is relatively **more gram-negative and polymicrobial**, because decolonization removes *S. aureus* selectively. ciNPWT's relative risk is a pooled all-surgery estimate and is assumed here to apply **equally** to that residual pool. No evidence in the base supports or refutes that assumption. The `decol_residual_attenuated` row relaxes it directly (RR 0.85 applied to the residual pool) and is the pessimistic corner of this analysis. A second limitation: the decolonization OR and the *S. aureus* fraction come from different populations, and `f_sa_ssi` carries no reported CI, so all the uncertainty in the multiplier comes from the odds ratio (0.692-0.991).

### Break-even risk `p*` on both reporting conventions

*Threshold provenance -- two reporting conventions, do not conflate them.* `p*` is solved **locally in `run_scenarios.py`** (`run_threshold.py` owns `threshold_results.csv` and is the authoritative module for every published threshold; this local solve exists only because the decolonization band above is defined in terms of `p*`). **Both bases are persisted here, each one named**, because BUILD-CONTRACT section 10 ("BASIS LABELS -- added 2026-08-09") requires every published threshold to name its basis and makes the **reporting base case** the manuscript headline:

| Scenario | **Reporting base case (24 cycles, 3%/yr discounting, half-cycle correction) -- MANUSCRIPT HEADLINE** | Undiscounted, no half-cycle (BUILD-CONTRACT section-10 hand-calc cross-check only) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base case -- matched attributable SSI cost (Pennington [14], m_ssi_cost = 0.492) | **1.235%** (1.2352%) | 1.219% (1.2194%) |
| All-cause SSI cost, upper bound (Edmiston [12] at face value  m_ssi_cost = 1.000) | **0.658%** (0.6578%) | 0.650% (0.6496%) |

Every scenario row in this file is run on the **reporting base case**, so the reporting-basis column is the one that is like-for-like with everything else here and with Table 3 / Table 6: the manuscript's base-case-to-upper-bound pair is **1.235% -> 0.658%**. The upper-bound row sits BELOW the base case, which is the direction A2 established and is the whole reason Edmiston's all-cause increment is treated as a bound: a larger averted cost makes the device look like it pays off sooner. The undiscounted column exists for one purpose -- it is the only basis on which the closed-form hand calculation and the engine are commensurable. **Never pair a reporting-basis threshold with an undiscounted one in the same sentence.** Discounting raises the threshold by 1.29% at base and 1.26% under the all-cause bound, always in the same direction and for the same structural reason: the device toll falls at cycle 0 where the discount factor is exactly 1, while every benefit it buys -- the SSI cost tranches at months 1-15 and the QALYs across all 24 cycles -- is discounted.

## Budget impact

**How 'risk-targeted ciNPWT' is reported, and why.** The population distribution of predicted 90-day SSI risk is **unavailable**, so a separately modelled risk-targeted third arm would require inventing one. Instead, per the plan, risk-targeted use is reported as a **derived** result: per-stratum per-patient increments scaled by the number of patients treated, parameterized by the **proportion treated**. A programme that treats a proportion *f* of its cases at stratum risk *p* is **mathematically identical** to a third arm whose targeting rule selects exactly those patients -- and this way nothing is fabricated. Say it plainly; it is a modelling choice with a reason, not a shortcut.

Per-patient increments are the base case (24 cycles, 3%/yr discounting, 2025 USD). `inc_cost_total_usd` is the **budget line** -- negative means the programme saves money -- and `net_budget_impact_100k_usd` is the population INMB at $100,000/QALY. The ~$60 decolonization bundle is background in **both** arms and cancels, so it is not a ciNPWT budget line.

## Explicitly not run

- **`societal_perspective`** -- Societal perspective (productivity loss, patient/caregiver time, travel). NOT RUN -- no societal cost input exists anywhere in the parameter store. The declared perspective is the US commercial payer on a payments basis (Medicare is the alternative payer scenario above); adding productivity or caregiver costs would require inventing them. Direction if it were run is unambiguous: SSI carries substantial productivity loss that the payer perspective ignores, so a societal perspective would raise the cost per SSI averted and move the threshold DOWN, making ciNPWT look better. The payer perspective is therefore the conservative one. Documented as unrun and data-limited.
- **`risk_targeted_arm`** -- 'Risk-targeted ciNPWT' as a separately modelled third arm. NOT RUN BY DESIGN -- and this is a plan decision, not a limitation of this script. A third arm that treats only patients above a risk threshold requires the POPULATION DISTRIBUTION of predicted 90-day SSI risk, which does not exist in the evidence base. Rather than invent one, risk-targeted ciNPWT is reported as a DERIVED result: the per-stratum rows in this file plus `budget_impact.csv`, which is parameterized by the proportion of the programme treated. That is MATHEMATICALLY IDENTICAL to a third arm whose targeting rule selects the same proportion at the same risk, and it avoids fabricating a distribution.

## What these scenarios do and do not carry

- **Verified.** Phase A2 full-text verification completed 2026-08-17: 46 of 48 parameters are closed out against the 14 source full texts and 43 carry a table/page locator. Only 2 still carry `verify=True` -- the ciNPWT institutional net acquisition price and the superficial tunnel length -- because no available source resolves either.
- **The parameter store is never mutated.** Every scenario is a fresh `sample` dict (`P()`) plus a fresh run-kwargs dict (`S()`); a snapshot of all 48 `Param.value`s is compared before and after the run and a mismatch raises.
- **Cost is incremental-versus-no-SSI**, not total cost of care. There is no index-surgery and no well-state cost by design -- the index fusion, implant, ward stay and routine follow-up cancel exactly between arms.
- **Scenarios are one-at-a-time** except where a joint scenario is defined (`horizon_5y_residual_decrement`, `decol_residual_attenuated`). They are not a probabilistic statement; `run_psa.py` carries that. Note in particular that `m_ssi_cost` is `fixed` and is **not** sampled in the PSA, so attribution uncertainty lives entirely in the `allcause_edmiston` scenario and in the DSA.
- **No Medicare tranche is extrapolated any more** (A2 -- see above); the attribution factor remains a Medicare-basis ratio applied to commercial tranches, which is a transfer and is labelled as one.
- **`icer` is `NaN` wherever ciNPWT is dominant**, which is most of this panel. That is the engine's design, not a failure; report `dominance` / `quadrant`.
